subtype: Sudden shifts in taste and friends [Observer]
passage: Note for Thursday's meeting with the school counsellor, from Pallavi. My son Kunal has started saying "cringe" and "no cap" at dinner, pushes his hair over his eyes, and plays a band I do not know. Three new friends, Arjun, Dev and Sameer, come by after school. On Monday I said, "What is this noise?" and Kunal went silent and shut his door. On Tuesday I asked him to play me his favourite song in the car and tell me what he likes in it. He explained for ten minutes, and even sang a line. I will keep asking about the friends, and not laugh at the words.

qa.q: What did Pallavi ask Kunal to do in the car?
qa.a: Pallavi asked Kunal to play his favourite song and tell what he likes in it.

qa.q: How might Kunal have felt when Pallavi said "What is this noise?" on Monday?
qa.a: Kunal likely felt mocked and hurt, which is why Kunal went silent and shut the door; ridicule pushes a teen closer to the group that accepts the new taste.

qa.q: What choice did Pallavi make on Tuesday that worked better than ridicule?
qa.a: Pallavi asked with curiosity and listened, which let Kunal explain for ten minutes and sing a line.

qa.q: How might Pallavi have felt when Kunal explained the band for ten minutes and even sang a line?
qa.a: Pallavi probably felt relieved and closer to Kunal, which is why the note plans to keep asking about the friends and not laugh at the words.

grounding: A parent notices new slang, music and friends, and finds that steady curiosity works better than ridicule.

passage: Sunday night. My daughter Irawati came home with a new phrase, "that's so mid", and a new circle from art class, Meher and Ishaan and a girl everyone calls Sunny. They hummed a song I have never heard. At lunch I laughed and said, "Mid? Like middle?" Her fork stopped. She took her plate to her room. I felt stupid. Tonight I knocked and asked her to teach me three of the new words. She rolled her eyes, but she taught me, and then told me Meher does funny voices and Ishaan draws maps of imaginary towns. Note to self: ask, do not mock. She is still the same girl. — Sangeeta

qa.q: Which phrase did Irawati bring home?
qa.a: Irawati brought home the phrase "that's so mid".

qa.q: What was Sangeeta feeling after Irawati took her plate to her room?
qa.a: Sangeeta felt stupid and regretful about having laughed; the knock on the door that night shows a wish to repair it.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta do that opened the conversation, and why did it work?
qa.a: Sangeeta knocked and asked Irawati to teach three new words, which shows interest instead of ridicule and lets Irawati be the expert.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Irawati when Sangeeta laughed at "mid" in front of everyone at lunch?
qa.a: Irawati probably felt embarrassed and dismissed, which fits stopping the fork and leaving the table; a new identity is easily hurt by mockery.

grounding: A parent notices new slang and a new social circle, and curiosity works better than ridicule, which pushes the teen away.
